stem: A Jest + React Testing Library suite cannot render `export default async function Page()` from the App Router. What does the Next.js testing guide recommend?

options.text: Wrap the async page in `<Suspense>` inside `render()` so Jest waits for the data to resolve
options.why: Jest does not support async Server Components; a Suspense wrapper does not change that.

options.text: Cover async Server Components with E2E tests; unit-test the synchronous ones
options.why: The docs say Jest and Vitest do not support async Server Components yet and recommend E2E tests for them.

options.text: Switch Jest to `testEnvironment: "node"` so it can run Server Components
options.why: The environment is not the problem; the test tools do not support async components at all yet.

options.text: Add `'use client'` to the page while testing so it renders on the client
options.why: That changes what you are testing, and a Client Component cannot be async anyway.

explanation: Since `async` Server Components are new to the React ecosystem, Jest and Vitest do not support rendering them. The Next.js docs recommend running unit tests for synchronous Server and Client Components and using end-to-end tests (Playwright or Cypress) for `async` components.

stem: Which three things does `next/jest` configure for you automatically? (Choose three.)

options.text: Transforms code with the Next.js Compiler (SWC)
options.why: next/jest sets up `transform` using the Next.js Compiler.

options.text: Auto-mocks stylesheets, image imports and `next/font`
options.why: CSS, CSS Modules (and Sass variants), images and next/font are mocked automatically.

options.text: Loads `.env` files (and their variants) into `process.env`
options.why: next/jest loads the .env family so code that reads env vars works in tests.

options.text: Starts a production server so tests can hit real routes
options.why: next/jest configures unit and component tests; it does not run your app.

options.text: Makes async Server Components renderable in jsdom
options.why: Jest still does not support async Server Components.

options.text: Mocks `fetch` globally to return empty JSON
options.why: next/jest does not mock network calls; that is up to your test setup.

explanation: Under the hood `next/jest` sets up the SWC transform, auto-mocks stylesheets, image imports and next/font, loads `.env` variants into `process.env`, ignores `node_modules` and `.next` from resolving and transforms, and loads `next.config.js` for flags that enable SWC transforms.

stem: A Playwright suite passes when run against `next dev`, yet a bug that only appears in production slips through. What does the Next.js testing guide recommend?

options.text: Run Playwright in Chromium only, since Firefox and WebKit add false failures
options.why: Playwright drives all three engines on purpose; dropping two does not catch production bugs.

options.text: Run the E2E tests against a production build started with `next build` and `next start`
options.why: The guide recommends testing production code so the app behaves as it will for users.

options.text: Mock the Next.js server with MSW so the E2E suite no longer needs any running Next.js app
options.why: E2E tests need the real server; mocking it removes what they are meant to check.

options.text: Switch to Vitest browser mode, because Playwright cannot drive Next.js apps
options.why: Playwright is one of the documented E2E tools for Next.js.

explanation: Playwright and Cypress need a running Next.js server. The docs recommend running tests against your production code (`npm run build` then `npm run start`) to more closely resemble how the app behaves, because development mode differs in rendering, caching and bundling. Playwright's `webServer` option can start the server for you.

stem: Cypress Component Testing can mount an `async` Server Component directly as long as you wrap it in `<Suspense>`.

options.text: True
options.why: The docs state that Cypress does not support Component Testing for async Server Components.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Cypress currently cannot component-test async Server Components, so the docs recommend E2E tests for them.

explanation: Cypress supports both E2E and Component Testing, but its Component Testing does not support `async` Server Components. Use Cypress (or Playwright) E2E tests against a running app for those.

stem: You set up Vitest for a Next.js app following the docs. Which `vitest.config.mts` makes React component tests render?

options.text: `test: { environment: "node" }` with the `next/jest` transform for JSX
options.why: next/jest is for Jest, and a node environment has no DOM for components to render into.

options.text: `test: { environment: "edge-runtime" }`, since App Router components run on the edge
options.why: Components do not run on the edge by default, and that environment has no DOM either.

options.text: `plugins: [tsconfigPaths(), react()]` and `test: { environment: "jsdom" }`
options.why: The docs add @vitejs/plugin-react for JSX and jsdom as the DOM environment.

options.text: No environment setting, because Vitest renders into a real browser by default
options.why: Vitest defaults to a node environment, so the docs set jsdom explicitly.

explanation: The documented setup installs `vitest`, `@vitejs/plugin-react`, `jsdom`, Testing Library and `vite-tsconfig-paths`, then exports `defineConfig({ plugins: [tsconfigPaths(), react()], test: { environment: 'jsdom' } })`. Like Jest, Vitest does not support async Server Components, so cover those with E2E tests.

stem: Match each kind of test with what it checks, as defined in the Next.js testing guide.

options.text: Unit test
Component test
Integration test
End-to-end test

prompts.text: A single function, hook or component in isolation
How a React component renders and responds to props and user events
How several units, such as components, hooks and functions, work together
A whole user flow, such as sign-up, in a browser against a production-like app

explanation: The guide distinguishes unit, component, integration, end-to-end and snapshot testing. Unit and component tests isolate small pieces; integration tests combine units; E2E tests run real user flows in a browser against a production-like environment.

stem: Two components each import their own `.module.css` file, and both files define a `.button` class. What happens?

options.text: The later import overrides the earlier one, so both components end up with the same styles
options.why: That is how two global stylesheets behave, not CSS Modules.

options.text: Each file gets a unique generated class name, so the styles do not collide
options.why: CSS Modules scope class names locally by generating unique names.

options.text: The build fails with a duplicate class name error
options.why: Reusing a class name across modules is exactly what CSS Modules allow.

options.text: Both classes are merged into one global `.button` rule
options.why: Module classes are not global; each import gets its own hashed name.

explanation: CSS Modules locally scope CSS by generating unique class names, so the same class can appear in different files without naming collisions. Import the module with `import styles from './button.module.css'` and use `styles.button`.

stem: In a production build, how does Next.js decide the order of the CSS it outputs?

options.text: Alphabetically by file name, so `a.module.css` always loads first
options.why: File names have no effect on order.

options.text: Global stylesheets always come after every CSS Module
options.why: There is no fixed global-after-module rule; import order decides.

options.text: By the order the stylesheets are imported in your code
options.why: The docs say CSS order depends on the order you import styles.

options.text: Smallest files first, to speed up the first paint
options.why: Size is not used to order CSS.

explanation: Next.js merges and chunks stylesheets during production builds, and the order of your CSS follows the order you import styles in your code. For example, a component's module imported before `page.module.css` is ordered before it. CSS order can differ in development, so check the final order with `next build`.

stem: Which two practices does Next.js recommend for keeping CSS ordering predictable? (Choose two.)

options.text: Import global styles and Tailwind stylesheets at the root of the app
options.why: Keeping global CSS in one place avoids order conflicts.

options.text: Use CSS Modules for component styles when Tailwind utilities are not enough
options.why: Scoped modules avoid clashing with global rules.

options.text: Import global CSS inside each page so it loads only where needed
options.why: Stylesheets are not removed on navigation, so scattered global CSS causes conflicts.

options.text: Reuse the same class names across modules so they share styles
options.why: Module class names are hashed, so this neither shares styles nor helps ordering.

options.text: Check the final CSS order in `next dev`, since the build keeps it
options.why: Order can differ in development; the docs say to verify with `next build`.

explanation: To keep ordering predictable the docs recommend importing global styles and Tailwind at the root, using Tailwind for most styling, using CSS Modules for component-specific styles, naming modules consistently, and optionally tuning `cssChunking`. Development can order CSS differently from the build, so verify with `next build`.

stem: Which setup matches the Next.js docs for adding Tailwind CSS (v4) to an App Router project?

options.text: Add `@tailwind base`, `components` and `utilities` to every CSS Module
options.why: Tailwind is imported once into the global stylesheet, not per module.

options.text: Set `tailwind: true` in `next.config.ts`; Next.js then compiles Tailwind classes with no extra packages
options.why: There is no such config option; Tailwind runs through PostCSS.

options.text: Import `tailwindcss/tailwind.css` at the top of each Client Component
options.why: That repeats global CSS in components and is not the documented setup.

options.text: Add `@tailwindcss/postcss` to PostCSS and `@import "tailwindcss"` in the root global CSS
options.why: That is the documented v4 setup, with the global CSS imported in the root layout.

explanation: Install `tailwindcss` and `@tailwindcss/postcss`, add the plugin to your PostCSS config, write `@import 'tailwindcss';` in the global CSS file, and import that file in the root layout. Older-browser projects can follow the separate Tailwind v3 guide.

stem: A component needs the value of the Sass variable `$primary-color` in JavaScript. Which setup does Next.js support?

options.text: Import a plain `variables.scss` file, and every Sass variable in it becomes a named JavaScript export
options.why: Plain Sass files are global CSS and do not export values to JavaScript.

options.text: Add `:export { primaryColor: $primary-color }` to `variables.module.scss` and import it
options.why: Next.js supports Sass variables exported from CSS Module files.

options.text: Read it from `process.env` after declaring it in `sassOptions`
options.why: sassOptions configure the compiler; they do not create environment variables.

options.text: Use `sassOptions.additionalData` to inject it into every component's props
options.why: additionalData prepends Sass code; it does not pass values to React.

explanation: Next.js supports Sass variables exported from CSS Module files. Declare `:export { primaryColor: $primary-color; }` in a `.module.scss` file, then `import variables from './variables.module.scss'` and read `variables.primaryColor`.

stem: By default, which npm package does Next.js use to compile Sass? (You can switch it with `sassOptions.implementation`.) Type the package name.
explanation: Next.js has built-in Sass support once a Sass package is installed, and by default it uses the `sass` package. Set `sassOptions: { implementation: 'sass-embedded' }` to use a different implementation.

stem: An App Router app uses styled-components. On the first page load, content flashes unstyled before the styles apply. What is the documented fix?

options.text: Convert the styled components into Server Components so styles render on the server
options.why: CSS-in-JS libraries are supported in Client Components, not Server Components.

options.text: Add a Client Component style registry using `useServerInsertedHTML` and wrap the root layout with it
options.why: The registry collects the rules during server rendering and inserts them before the content.

options.text: Load each styled component with `next/dynamic` and `ssr: false` so the styles and the markup always arrive together
options.why: That removes server rendering of the content entirely instead of fixing style injection.

options.text: Move all styles into one global stylesheet imported in each page component
options.why: That abandons CSS-in-JS rather than configuring it, and scattered global CSS causes conflicts.

explanation: CSS-in-JS in the App Router needs three parts: a style registry that collects CSS rules during a render, the `useServerInsertedHTML` hook to inject those rules before the content that uses them, and a Client Component that wraps the app with the registry during server rendering. The docs show this for styled-jsx and styled-components.

stem: According to the Next.js docs, `emotion` is already supported in Client Components in the `app` directory.

options.text: True
options.why: Emotion is not in the supported list.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the docs list emotion under libraries still "working on support".

explanation: The docs list libraries that work in Client Components in the `app` directory, such as styled-components, styled-jsx, MUI, Chakra UI, Panda CSS and vanilla-extract. Emotion is listed separately as currently working on support. All of them run in Client Components, not Server Components.

stem: After installing `@next/mdx` and adding `md` and `mdx` to `pageExtensions`, `app/blog/page.mdx` still does not work in the App Router. What is missing?

options.text: A `pages/_app.mdx` file that wraps every MDX page
options.why: There is no such file convention, and pages/ is the Pages Router.

options.text: A `'use client'` directive on the first line of the MDX file
options.why: MDX works in Server Components, which are the App Router default.

options.text: An `mdx-components.tsx` file at the project root, or in `src/`
options.why: The docs say this file is required for @next/mdx with the App Router.

options.text: Renaming the file to `page.md`, since `.mdx` pages are not routable
options.why: `.mdx` pages are supported once pageExtensions includes `mdx`.

explanation: `mdx-components.tsx` (or `.js`) is required to use `@next/mdx` with the App Router and will not work without it. Put it at the project root, beside `app`, or inside `src` if you use one. It defines global MDX components, and `pageExtensions` must include `md`/`mdx` for MDX pages.

stem: An app uses `@next/mdx` with `pageExtensions` that include `md`. Pages written as `page.mdx` render, but `page.md` files are ignored. Why?

options.text: `@next/mdx` compiles only `.mdx` by default; change its `extension` option to include `.md`
options.why: The docs say @next/mdx only compiles .mdx unless you update the extension option.

options.text: Next.js treats `.md` files as plain text, so they can never be routed as pages in either router
options.why: Markdown pages work once @next/mdx is configured to compile them.

options.text: `.md` pages only work in the Pages Router, so they must move to `pages/`
options.why: Both routers support MDX through the same plugin.

options.text: `pageExtensions` needs the value `markdown`, not `md`
options.why: The extension list uses `md`; the problem is the plugin's default file filter.

explanation: By default `@next/mdx` only compiles files with the `.mdx` extension. To process `.md` files too, update the plugin's `extension` option, as the docs show for webpack. `pageExtensions` only controls which files Next.js considers as pages.

stem: `@next/mdx` is the right tool for rendering MDX that a Server Component fetches from a CMS at request time.

options.text: True
options.why: @next/mdx compiles local files at build time.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the docs say @next/mdx sources data from local files; remote MDX needs a runtime compiler.

explanation: `@next/mdx` sources data from local files and compiles `.mdx` (and optionally `.md`) pages and imports in your project. MDX fetched dynamically, for example from a CMS, has to be compiled at runtime with a remote-MDX library instead.

stem: Where do you call `registerOTel({ serviceName: "next-app" })` from `@vercel/otel`?

options.text: At the top of `app/layout.tsx`, so tracing starts before any page in the app is rendered
options.why: Layouts render per request; instrumentation needs a one-time server hook.

options.text: Inside the `proxy` function in `proxy.ts`
options.why: Proxy runs per request and is not the documented setup hook.

options.text: In `next.config.ts`, inside an `experimental.otel` block
options.why: There is no such config; setup happens in the instrumentation file.

options.text: Inside the `register` function exported from `instrumentation.ts` at the project root
options.why: register() runs once when the server starts, which is where tracing is set up.

explanation: Create `instrumentation.ts` in the root of the project, or inside `src` alongside `app`, but not inside `app` or `pages`. Export a `register` function that calls `registerOTel`. If you use a `pageExtensions` suffix, the instrumentation file name must use it too.

stem: Which two statements about OpenTelemetry in Next.js are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Next.js already instruments itself and emits spans for things like route rendering
options.why: The docs say Next.js supports OpenTelemetry out of the box and wraps its own work in spans.

options.text: With a `pageExtensions` suffix such as `page.tsx`, the instrumentation file name must use it too
options.why: The docs call out updating the file name to match the suffix.

options.text: OpenTelemetry tracing only works for apps deployed on Vercel
options.why: @vercel/otel is a helper package; OpenTelemetry works with any OTLP-compatible backend.

options.text: `instrumentation.ts` must live inside the `app` directory
options.why: It must be at the project root (or in src/), not inside app or pages.

options.text: No spans are emitted until you add manual spans to every route
options.why: Built-in spans are emitted once instrumentation is registered.

explanation: Next.js ships with its own OpenTelemetry instrumentation, wrapping rendering and data fetching in spans. `@vercel/otel` is a convenience package for setup, called from `register()` in `instrumentation.ts`, which lives at the root or in `src`, outside `app` and `pages`, and follows any `pageExtensions` suffix.

stem: A hero section uses `<video src="/hero.mp4" autoPlay loop />`. It autoplays on desktop but not on iPhones. Which change fixes it?

options.text: Render the video through `next/image` so Next.js optimizes it
options.why: next/image handles images, not video playback.

options.text: Set `preload="auto"` so the browser downloads the whole file first
options.why: Preloading does not lift browser autoplay restrictions.

options.text: Add `muted` and `playsInline`
options.why: Autoplay usually needs muted, and iOS Safari needs playsInline for inline autoplay.

options.text: Wrap the video in `<Suspense>` with a poster image as the fallback
options.why: Suspense handles data loading in React; it does not affect autoplay rules.

explanation: Browsers restrict autoplay. `muted` is commonly needed alongside `autoPlay`, and `playsInline` enables inline playback on iOS, which is often necessary for autoplay to work in iOS Safari. Add `poster` and `preload="none"` or `"metadata"` to control what loads before playback.

stem: A page embeds a third-party video with `<iframe src="…" loading="lazy" />` and no size. When the iframe loads late, the content below it jumps. What does the Next.js video guide recommend?

options.text: Give the iframe a `width` and `height`, or an `aspect-ratio`
options.why: An unsized iframe collapses until its content loads, which causes the shift.

options.text: Remove `loading="lazy"` so the iframe loads during hydration
options.why: Eager loading wastes bandwidth and still shifts if the box has no size.

options.text: Wrap the iframe in `next/image` so its dimensions are measured at build time
options.why: next/image is for images and cannot wrap an iframe.

options.text: Load the iframe with `next/dynamic` and `ssr: false`
options.why: Client-only rendering does not reserve space and can make the shift worse.

explanation: An iframe without dimensions collapses until its content loads, just like a video. Reserve space with `width` and `height` or an `aspect-ratio`, particularly with `loading="lazy"`, where the embed can resolve long after the page paints. For platform embeds, the guide also shows a Server Component that fetches the embed details, streamed inside `<Suspense>` with a skeleton fallback.

stem: You want Google Tag Manager on every route using `@next/third-parties`. Where should `<GoogleTagManager gtmId="GTM-XYZ" />` go?

options.text: In `proxy.ts`, so it is injected into every response
options.why: Proxy cannot render React components into pages.

options.text: In the root layout
options.why: Rendering it in the root layout loads the container for all routes.

options.text: In every `page.tsx`, because layouts cannot render third-party components
options.why: Layouts can render it, and the root layout covers every route at once.

options.text: In `next.config.ts` under a `thirdParties` key
options.why: There is no config key; the library is used as React components.

explanation: To load Google Tag Manager on all routes, include `<GoogleTagManager />` directly in the root layout and pass your container ID. To load it on a single route, render it in that page instead. By default it fetches the GTM script after the page hydrates.

stem: `@next/third-parties` is a stable library, so the docs recommend pinning it to the stable release channel.

options.text: True
options.why: The docs describe it as experimental.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the docs call it experimental and suggest installing the latest or canary version.

explanation: `@next/third-parties` is currently an experimental library under active development. The docs recommend installing it with the `latest` or `canary` tag while more integrations are added.

stem: Which two points come from the Next.js production checklist? (Choose two.)

options.text: Reading `cookies()` or `searchParams` in the root layout makes the whole app render dynamically
options.why: The checklist warns that request-time APIs opt the route, or the whole app from the root layout, into dynamic rendering.

options.text: Run Lighthouse in incognito and pair it with field data such as Core Web Vitals
options.why: The checklist calls Lighthouse a simulated test to combine with real-user data.

options.text: Call your own Route Handlers from Server Components to reuse API logic
options.why: The checklist says not to, because it adds an extra server request.

options.text: Commit `.env.local` so CI builds have the same secrets
options.why: The checklist says to keep `.env.*` files in .gitignore.

options.text: Confirm the final CSS order in `next dev`
options.why: CSS order can differ in development; verify it with `next build`.

explanation: The checklist covers routing and rendering (layouts, Link, error pages, intentional use of request-time APIs wrapped in Suspense), data fetching (fetch in Server Components, do not call Route Handlers from Server Components, parallel fetching, caching), security (taint, auth in Server Actions, `.env*` in .gitignore, CSP), metadata, and performance checks such as Lighthouse in incognito alongside Core Web Vitals.

stem: A platform team writes a Next.js deployment adapter. After the build, it needs the routing table and the list of prerendered outputs to configure its CDN. Which adapter hook provides them?

options.text: `modifyConfig`
options.why: modifyConfig runs when next.config is loaded and lets you change the config; it gets no build outputs.

options.text: `onBuildComplete`
options.why: It is called after the build with `routing` and `outputs`, including prerenders.

options.text: `register` in `instrumentation.ts`
options.why: That hook runs when the server starts, not after a build.

options.text: `generateBuildId`
options.why: It only returns the build ID string.

explanation: A Next.js adapter implements `modifyConfig(config, { phase, nextVersion, projectDir })`, called for any CLI command that loads next.config, and `onBuildComplete({ routing, outputs, ... })`, called after the build. The latter receives the routing phases, middleware matchers and dynamic routes, plus outputs such as pages, App Router pages, API routes and prerenders.

stem: A hosting platform wants to apply its Next.js adapter without asking users to edit `next.config.ts`. What does Next.js support for that?

options.text: Setting `output: "adapter"` from the platform's build image
options.why: There is no `adapter` output mode.

options.text: Passing `next build --adapter ./adapter.js`
options.why: There is no such CLI flag.

options.text: An `adapters` field in the project's `package.json`
options.why: Next.js does not read adapters from package.json.

options.text: Setting the `NEXT_ADAPTER_PATH` environment variable
options.why: The docs describe this env var for zero-config adapter use on deployment platforms.

explanation: You can point Next.js at an adapter with `adapterPath` in next.config, for example `require.resolve('./my-adapter.js')`, or set `NEXT_ADAPTER_PATH`. The env var enables zero-config usage on deployment platforms.

stem: A CI script scaffolds a project with `create-next-app` and must not stop at interactive prompts. Which flag uses previous preferences or the defaults for every option?

options.text: `--empty`
options.why: --empty initialises an empty project; it does not skip the prompts.

options.text: `--skip-install`
options.why: That skips installing packages, not the questions.

options.text: `--yes`
options.why: --yes uses previous preferences or defaults for all options.

options.text: `--reset-preferences`
options.why: That clears stored preferences; it does not answer prompts.

explanation: `create-next-app --yes` answers every prompt with your previous preferences or the defaults, which suits automation. The recommended defaults are TypeScript, ESLint, Tailwind CSS, the App Router and AGENTS.md, with Turbopack enabled.

stem: Which of these is NOT part of `create-next-app`'s recommended defaults?

options.text: TypeScript (instead of JavaScript)
options.why: TypeScript is a recommended default.

options.text: Tailwind CSS for styling
options.why: Tailwind CSS is a recommended default.

options.text: The App Router
options.why: The App Router is a recommended default.

options.text: A `src/` directory
options.why: src/ is opt-in with `--src-dir`; it is not in the recommended defaults.

explanation: The "recommended Next.js defaults" prompt lists TypeScript, ESLint, Tailwind CSS, the App Router and AGENTS.md, and Turbopack is enabled by default. A `src/` directory is opt-in via `--src-dir`, and options such as `--react-compiler`, `--biome` or `--api` are also opt-in.

stem: A team runs Next.js through a custom Express `server.js` and wants to add `output: "standalone"` to shrink their Docker image. What should they know?

options.text: Standalone output wraps the custom server automatically and keeps all of its Express routes and middleware working
options.why: Standalone emits its own server.js and does not trace custom server files.

options.text: They can't be combined: standalone emits its own `server.js` and doesn't trace custom server files
options.why: The docs state that standalone output and a custom server cannot be used together.

options.text: They must also compile `server.js` with the Next.js compiler using `transpilePackages`
options.why: server.js never goes through the Next.js compiler, and transpilePackages is unrelated.

options.text: It works as long as the custom server listens on port 3000
options.why: The port is not the issue; the two deployment modes are incompatible.

explanation: With standalone output, Next.js traces only what its own minimal `server.js` needs, so custom server files are not traced and the two cannot be used together. A custom `server.js` also does not run through the Next.js compiler or bundler, so its syntax must suit your Node.js version.

stem: A CI build of a large Next.js app runs out of memory. Which built-in option prints heap and garbage-collection statistics during the build and takes heap snapshots as memory nears the limit?

options.text: `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192`
options.why: This raises the heap limit but reports nothing about where memory goes.

options.text: `next build --experimental-debug-memory-usage`
options.why: It prints heap and GC stats and takes snapshots near the configured limit.

options.text: `experimental.webpackMemoryOptimizations: true`
options.why: This reduces webpack memory use but does not print diagnostics.

options.text: `next build --profile`
options.why: That flag profiles React rendering in production, not build memory.

explanation: Since 14.2, `next build --experimental-debug-memory-usage` prints memory information throughout the build, such as heap usage and GC statistics, and takes heap snapshots automatically when usage nears the limit. Sending `SIGUSR2` to the process takes a snapshot on demand. Other strategies include analysing dependencies with the bundle analyzer and recording a heap profile with `node --heap-prof`.

stem: While `next build --experimental-debug-memory-usage` runs, sending `SIGUSR2` to the process writes a heap snapshot to the project root.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the docs say SIGUSR2 triggers a heap snapshot saved in the project root.

options.text: False
options.why: This is documented behaviour of the debug memory mode.

explanation: In this mode you can send a `SIGUSR2` signal at any point, and the process takes a heap snapshot saved to the project root. You can then load it in Chrome DevTools or another heap analyzer to see what memory is retained. The mode is not yet compatible with webpack build workers.

stem: A developer adds custom module declarations to `next-env.d.ts`. After the next `next dev` run, they are gone. What should they do?

options.text: Mark the file read-only so that Next.js can no longer overwrite it during `next dev`
options.why: Next.js manages the file; blocking regeneration breaks its type references.

options.text: Move the declarations into `next.config.ts`
options.why: Config files do not provide ambient type declarations.

options.text: Put them in a separate `.d.ts` file, because Next.js regenerates `next-env.d.ts`
options.why: next-env.d.ts is managed by Next.js and must not be edited manually.

options.text: Remove `next-env.d.ts` from the `tsconfig.json` include array
options.why: The file must stay in `include`; removing it loses Next.js types.

explanation: Next.js generates `next-env.d.ts`, which references its type definitions so TypeScript understands image and stylesheet imports and Next.js types. `next dev`, `next build` and `next typegen` regenerate it, so add it to .gitignore, never edit it by hand, and keep it in the tsconfig `include` array. Put your own declarations in a separate `.d.ts` file.

stem: In a project not created with `create-next-app`, a developer enables `typedRoutes: true`, but `<Link href="/no-such-page">` still compiles without an error. What is the likely fix?

options.text: Also set `experimental.typedLinks: true` in `next.config.ts` alongside typedRoutes
options.why: There is no such option; typedRoutes is the switch.

options.text: Add `.next/types/**/*.ts` to the `include` array in `tsconfig.json`
options.why: The docs say projects set up manually must include the generated Next.js types.

options.text: Rename the route files from `.tsx` to `.ts` so they can be typed
options.why: Pages stay `.tsx`; the generated route types are what is missing.

options.text: Typed links only work in Client Components, so add `'use client'`
options.why: Typed routes apply wherever Link is used.

explanation: Statically typed links need TypeScript and `typedRoutes: true`. Next.js generates route types under `.next/types`. `create-next-app` includes them automatically, but a manually set-up project must add `.next/types/**/*.ts` to `tsconfig.json` `include`, or the types are never checked.

stem: A Pages Router route uses `getStaticPaths` with `fallback: true`. What does a first-time visitor to a path that was not generated at build time get, and what does a search crawler get?

options.text: Both get a 404 until the next build adds the path
options.why: That is fallback: false; with true, missing paths are generated on demand.

options.text: Both get the fallback loading UI, then the page swaps in once props are ready
options.why: Crawlers are not served the fallback; they get the blocking behaviour.

options.text: The visitor sees the fallback version first; the crawler is served as if `fallback: "blocking"`
options.why: The docs say crawlers such as Google are not served a fallback.

options.text: Both wait for a fully server-rendered page first, exactly as they would with `fallback: "blocking"`
options.why: For regular visitors, true serves the fallback page first.

explanation: With `fallback: true`, ungenerated paths do not 404. The first request gets a fallback version, where `router.isFallback` is true, while `getStaticProps` runs, and the generated page is cached for later requests. Web crawlers are not served a fallback and behave as with `"blocking"`, as do client-side navigations through next/link. Neither `true` nor `"blocking"` works with `output: "export"`.

stem: In the Pages Router, a blog post has been deleted. Which key, set to `true` in the object returned from `getServerSideProps`, makes Next.js respond with the 404 page? Type the key.
explanation: Return `{ notFound: true }` from `getServerSideProps` (or `getStaticProps`) to respond with a 404 status and the 404 page. To send users elsewhere, return `{ redirect: { destination, permanent } }`; use `statusCode` instead of `permanent` for older clients, but never both.

stem: A Pages Router app adds `getInitialProps` to `pages/_app.tsx` to load the current user for every page. What side effect does this have?

options.text: None, because data fetching in `_app` runs only once at build time and then gets cached
options.why: getInitialProps runs per request on the server, and again on client navigations.

options.text: It disables Automatic Static Optimization for pages without `getStaticProps`
options.why: The docs say getInitialProps in App opts those pages out of static optimization.

options.text: It turns every page into a Client Component
options.why: Pages Router pages are not Server or Client Components in the App Router sense.

options.text: Next.js ignores it, because `_app` can't fetch data
options.why: `_app` does not support getStaticProps or getServerSideProps, but getInitialProps does run.

explanation: Using `getInitialProps` in a custom App disables Automatic Static Optimization for pages that do not use `getStaticProps`, so they are rendered on every request. `App` does not support `getStaticProps` or `getServerSideProps`, and the docs recommend moving such logic to the App Router rather than using this pattern.

stem: In a Pages Router app, a developer adds a button with an `onClick` handler to `pages/_document.tsx`. The handler never fires. Why?

options.text: `_document` only supports class components, and class components can't use event handlers
options.why: Function components work; the problem is where the file renders.

options.text: Event handlers in `_document` need a `"use client"` directive
options.why: Directives are an App Router concept and would not help here.

options.text: The handler must be passed through `pageProps` from `_app`
options.why: _app props cannot make server-only document markup interactive.

options.text: `_document` renders only on the server; nothing outside `<Main />` is hydrated
options.why: The docs say event handlers cannot be used in this file.

explanation: `_document` customises the `<html>` and `<body>` tags and renders only on the server. React components outside `<Main />` are not initialised in the browser, so event handlers and application logic do not belong there. Shared UI such as menus goes in a layout used from `_app`.

stem: In the Pages Router, page-specific `<title>` tags belong in the `<Head />` component of `pages/_document.tsx`.

options.text: True
options.why: The _document Head is for head content shared by all pages.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the docs say to use `next/head` in pages or components for titles.

explanation: The `<Head />` from `next/document` is not the same as `next/head`. It should only hold `<head>` content common to every page. For per-page tags such as `<title>`, use `next/head` in your pages or components. In the App Router, the Metadata API replaces both.

stem: A Pages Router page has no `getServerSideProps`, `getStaticProps` or `getInitialProps`, and `_app` has no `getInitialProps` either. How is it rendered in production?

options.text: Server-rendered on every request, because a page without a data method can't be prerendered
options.why: Pages without blocking data requirements are prerendered, not rendered per request.

options.text: Rendered only in the browser, with an empty HTML shell
options.why: Next.js still prerenders the page to HTML.

options.text: Prerendered to static HTML at build time (Automatic Static Optimization)
options.why: Next.js detects that the page has no blocking data requirements and serves it statically.

options.text: Regenerated every 60 seconds with ISR by default
options.why: ISR only applies when getStaticProps returns `revalidate`.

explanation: Automatic Static Optimization means a page with no blocking data requirements (no `getServerSideProps` or `getInitialProps`, including in `_app`) is prerendered to HTML at build time and can be served from a CDN. Adding `getServerSideProps`, or `getInitialProps` in `_app`, opts it into rendering on every request.

stem: You are building an SPA-style dashboard. A deep Client Component needs the current user, and you want the request to start as early as possible without a client-side waterfall. Which pattern does the Next.js SPA guide show?

options.text: Fetch the user in a `useEffect` in the deepest component that needs it
options.why: Fetching in an effect starts late, only after hydration, which creates a waterfall.

options.text: Start the fetch unawaited in the root layout, share the Promise via context, read it with `use()`
options.why: The request starts on the server early and streams to the Client Component.

options.text: Await the user in the root layout and pass it down as a prop through every component level below
options.why: Awaiting blocks the whole layout; the guide passes an unawaited Promise.

options.text: Call a Route Handler from the root layout and store the JSON in localStorage
options.why: Calling your own Route Handler from a Server Component adds a request, and localStorage is client-only.

explanation: Start the request in a Server Component such as the root layout without awaiting it, and pass the Promise to a context provider. Client Components then read it with React's `use()`, which they need because they cannot `await` during render. The response streams immediately and avoids client waterfalls. For polling, mutations or focus revalidation, the guide points to SWR or TanStack Query.

stem: What does Next.js add over a "strict" SPA that serves every route from a single `index.html`?

options.text: Automatic code splitting with separate HTML entry points per route, plus link prefetching
options.why: This loads less JavaScript per page while keeping fast transitions.

options.text: A requirement to render every route on the server for each request
options.why: Next.js can still run as a static site or fully client-rendered SPA.

options.text: Full-page reloads on navigation, so state always resets cleanly
options.why: Next.js uses client-side navigation, not full reloads.

options.text: One bundle that holds every route, so navigation never has to fetch any more JavaScript code
options.why: Next.js splits code per route instead of shipping one big bundle.

explanation: Strict SPAs often ship a lot of JavaScript before becoming interactive and suffer client data waterfalls. Next.js code-splits bundles and generates multiple HTML entry points per route, while `next/link` prefetching keeps transitions fast and routing state in the URL. You can start as a static site or strict SPA and add server features later.

options.text: Wrap each `await` in its own `try/catch` block
options.why: Error handling does not change when the requests start.

options.text: Move both calls into a `useEffect` so they run after the component has rendered
options.why: Server Components cannot use effects, and fetching on the client would be later still.

options.text: Add `"use cache"` so the second call waits less
options.why: Caching does not start the second request any earlier on a cache miss.

options.text: Start both calls first, then `await Promise.all([artistData, albumsData])`
options.why: Requests begin when the functions are called, so both run at the same time.

explanation: Within one component, consecutive `await`s are sequential: `getAlbums` is blocked until `getArtist` resolves. Initiate both requests (`const artistData = getArtist(id)`), then await them together with `Promise.all`. Layouts and pages in a route already render in parallel; this pattern handles requests inside one component.
reference: Next.js docs: Fetching Data (Parallel data fetching)

stem: When you fetch in parallel with `Promise.all` and one request rejects, the page still receives the results of the requests that succeeded.

options.text: True
options.why: Promise.all rejects as soon as any input rejects.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: with Promise.all one failure fails the whole operation; the docs suggest Promise.allSettled.

explanation: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as any request rejects, so the whole operation fails. The Next.js docs suggest `Promise.allSettled` when you want each result regardless of failures, then handle each fulfilled or rejected entry.
reference: Next.js docs: Fetching Data (Parallel data fetching)

stem: A page first awaits `checkIsAvailable()`, then renders `<Item id={id} />`, which loads its data with `getItem(id)`, an ORM query. `getItem` cannot start until the check finishes. Following the Next.js preloading pattern, how do you start `getItem` early?

options.text: Move `getItem` into a Route Handler and fetch it from `<Item>`
options.why: That adds an HTTP hop and still starts after the check.

options.text: Wrap `getItem` in `React.cache`, call it unawaited before the check, and call it again in `<Item>`
options.why: The early call starts the query, and React.cache lets the component reuse the same result.

options.text: Call `getItem` inside `<Item>` with `Promise.all` and an empty second promise
options.why: Promise.all inside Item still begins only after the parent finishes the check.

options.text: Mark the whole page with `"use cache"` so `getItem` is skipped on every request after the first one
options.why: That caches across requests, which is a different goal, and may serve stale data.

explanation: To preload, call the data function without `await` before the blocking work, then call the same function in the component that uses it. The function must deduplicate matching calls: use `fetch` memoization, or wrap ORM and database calls in `React.cache`, which is scoped to the current request. Keep a small `preload()` helper next to the consuming component.
